text: The Galápagos Islands, a volcanic archipelago in the Pacific Ocean 600 miles west of Ecuador, played a pivotal role in Charles Darwin's development of natural selection. Darwin visited aboard HMS Beagle in 1835 as the ship's naturalist, observing finches and tortoises that varied from island to island. He later published On the Origin of Species in 1859, which introduced the theory of evolution by natural selection. Alfred Russel Wallace independently conceived the same theory and corresponded with Darwin; their joint paper was read at the Linnean Society of London in 1858. Today, the Charles Darwin Foundation operates a research station on Santa Cruz Island to conserve the islands' unique biodiversity, including the Galápagos giant tortoise and the marine iguana. UNESCO designated the Galápagos as a World Heritage Site in 1978, though invasive species and tourism remain ongoing threats. The government of Ecuador established the Galápagos National Park in 1959 to protect the islands.
